title: Net product revenue by month in 2010

brief.decision: A take-home task from our hiring team in the Netherlands, on a public dataset, Online Retail II: how the shop's net product revenue moved month by month in 2010, once cancellations, postage and fees are taken out. Both of the source's sheets held December 2010, and the data keeps one copy of those lines; lines repeated within a sheet were kept as the source has them, so in this task a line that matches another line in every column counts once.

checkpoints.prompt: Noor wants the shop's net product revenue for each month of 2010 from Online Retail II, the invoice lines of a UK online gift shop. Many product lines have a missing customer ID. What should the revenue figures do with those lines?

options.text: Leave them out: a line with no customer ID cannot be traced to a buyer, so its sale is not safe to count.
Leave them out, since a missing customer ID marks a cancelled or test invoice rather than a real sale.
Keep them: they are sales like any other, and the customer ID only matters for questions about customers.
Fill each one in from another line of the same invoice, and leave out the lines that still have no customer ID.

checkpoints.prompt: In Online Retail II, take every invoice line dated in 2010, from 1 January to 31 December, whatever its stock code or invoice. Some lines match another line in every column, where a missing value matches a missing value in the same column. Keeping one line from each set of matching lines, how many lines are extra copies? Type a whole number.
Write the query that answers Noor's question.

In Online Retail II, take the product lines dated in 2010, from 1 January to 31 December: a product line is a line whose stock code starts with a digit. Count a line that matches another line in every column once, where a missing value matches a missing value. A line's value is its quantity times its price, in pounds sterling. A cancellation, an invoice whose number starts with C, has negative quantities, so its lines take value away. Lines with a missing customer ID count. What was the net product revenue for the whole year, the sum of the values of those lines? Type the amount in pounds sterling without the pound sign, rounded to 2 decimals.

In Noor's 2010 table from Online Retail II, the invoice lines of a UK online gift shop, net product revenue climbs from September to a peak in November, then falls by almost half in December. Nothing else has been checked yet. Noor asks: does the December fall mean the shop is losing customers?

options.text: Yes. Net revenue fell by almost half from November to December, and a fall that size means many customers stopped buying from the shop.
Not from this table. Gift buyers stock up before Christmas, so December can fall with the season; compare it with December 2009 and count each month's buyers first.
No. Both of the source's sheets held December 2010, so the fall only shows one copy of its lines being removed when the data was prepared.
No. A cancellation counts in the month it was made, so the December fall is only November's orders being cancelled in December.

checkpoints.prompt: Write 2 to 4 sentences for Noor: how the shop's net product revenue moved through 2010, how much cancellations took back, one caveat about the data, and one next step.

model_plan:
Metric formula: per month, sales_gbp adds quantity times price over the product lines of invoices that do not start with C; cancelled_gbp is minus the same sum over the invoices that start with C; net_revenue_gbp is sales_gbp minus cancelled_gbp; cancelled_pct is 100 times cancelled_gbp divided by sales_gbp, rounded to 1 decimal; the amounts are rounded to 2 decimals.
Output grain: one row per month of 2010.
Tables and keys: invoice_lines only, so there is no join.
Filters: invoice dates from 1 January 2010 up to, not including, 1 January 2011; stock codes that start with a digit; one copy of each set of lines that match in every column.
Edge cases: lines with a missing customer ID stay in; a cancellation counts in its own month, not the month of the sale it reverses; a stock adjustment with a negative quantity has price 0 and adds nothing; December 2010 already holds one copy of the lines both source sheets held.
Expected row count: 12
model_answer_template: In 2010 the shop's net product revenue, after cancellations and without postage, fees and adjustments, came to {CP4} pounds sterling, climbing from September to a peak in November before falling back in December. Cancellations took back a small share of sales in most months, and 2010 held {CP2} extra copies of lines that repeat another line in every column, which I counted once. The December fall looks like the end of the gift season rather than lost customers, so my next step is to compare it with December 2009 and count each month's buying customers.
follow_up_question: Does December's fall mean the shop is losing customers?
